entries_new.name: Virginia Company
entries_new.founder: Investors in London, chartered by the English king
entries_new.mechanism: A royal charter gave a joint-stock company the right to settle and govern a stretch of the North American coast.
entries_new.story: The Virginia Company was an English trading company that received a royal charter on 10 April 1606 to colonise the east coast of North America, a stretch named Virginia that ran from present-day Maine to the Carolinas. Its shareholders were Londoners. A separate company of Plymouth gentlemen was chartered at the same time. After a 1622 attack by Indigenous people killed many colonists, the company failed, and on 24 May 1624 the king dissolved it and made Virginia a royal colony. Colonists kept a lower house, the House of Burgesses.

entries_new.name: Council for New England
entries_new.founder: Sir Ferdinando Gorges was a key promoter
entries_new.mechanism: A royal charter gave a company the right to grant and settle land across a defined band of North America.
entries_new.story: The Council for New England was an English joint stock company that received a royal charter in November 1620 with the aim of extending the king's realm in North America through settlements. Its charter covered land between the 40th and 48th parallels, which the text describes as the part of the Virginia Colony north of the 40th parallel. It was disbanded in 1635, with no apparent change in land titles. It provided for the Plymouth Colony, the Province of New Hampshire, the Massachusetts Bay Colony, the New Haven Colony and the Province of Maine.

entries_new.name: Somers Isles Company
entries_new.stopped_by: Dissolved in 1684; the Crown took over
entries_new.mechanism: A royal charter gave a company the islands to run as a commercial venture.
entries_new.story: The Somers Isles Company was formed in 1615 to run Bermuda, also called the Somers Isles, as a commercial venture. The islands had been settled by accident in 1609, when the Virginia Company's flagship Sea Venture was wrecked on the reefs. The new company held a royal charter for Bermuda until 1684, when it was dissolved and the Crown took over the administration, making Bermuda a royal colony.

entries_new.name: Providence Island Company
entries_new.founder: Robert Rich, 2nd Earl of Warwick, and Puritan investors
entries_new.mechanism: A charter gave a group of investors a Caribbean island to settle and use as a privateering base.
entries_new.story: The Providence Island Company was an English company founded in 1629 by Puritan investors, among them Robert Rich, 2nd Earl of Warwick, to settle Providence Island, now part of Colombia's San Andrés y Providencia Department. Settlers ran plantations. The colonies also served as a base for privateers (ship owners licensed to attack an enemy's shipping) working against Spanish ships and settlements, with one fifth of plunder owed to the company. A patent was granted on 4 December 1630. The Spanish and Portuguese destroyed the colonies in 1641.

entries_new.name: Massachusetts Bay Company
entries_new.mechanism: A royal charter let a company's investors move to America and govern the colony themselves.
entries_new.story: The Massachusetts Bay Company was a joint-stock company set up by English royal charter that founded the Massachusetts Bay Colony in 1628, around Salem and Boston. The colony's nominal territory covered much of central New England. About 20,000 people migrated there in the 1630s, and governors were chosen by an electorate limited to freemen admitted to the local church. The colony took part in the Pequot War (1636 to 1638) and King Philip's War (1675 to 1678). In 1691 its territory was reorganised as the Province of Massachusetts Bay.

entries_new.name: Dutch West India Company
entries_new.mechanism: A state charter gave a company a trade monopoly and the right to hold and run overseas colonies.
entries_new.story: The Dutch West India Company was chartered on 3 June 1621 by the Republic of the Seven United Netherlands, with a trade monopoly across West Africa and the Americas and jurisdiction over Dutch participation in the Atlantic slave trade, Brazil, the Caribbean and North America. It founded New Netherland, which included New Amsterdam on Manhattan, and from 1624 to 1654 held part of northeast Brazil before being driven out. The first company dissolved in 1674 over debts. A second charter in 1675 lasted until 1792.

entries_new.name: Society of Berbice
entries_new.mechanism: Colony owners pooled capital into a share-issuing company that governed the colony.
entries_new.story: The Society of Berbice was founded on 24 October 1720 by five owners of the colony of Berbice, in present-day Guyana, who had bought it from the French in 1714. It was a public company listed on the Amsterdam Stock Exchange and raised capital for the colony, which at one point held 12 society plantations beside 93 private plantations on the Berbice River. A slave uprising under Coffy in February 1763 caused plantation losses and financial trouble. Berbice was ceded to Britain, the last plantations were sold in November 1818, and the offices closed in 1821.

entries_new.name: Society of Suriname
entries_new.mechanism: Three shareholders jointly ran a colony under a charter from the Dutch state.
entries_new.story: The Society of Suriname was a Dutch private company set up on 21 May 1683 to profit from the management and defence of the Dutch colony of Suriname. It had three equal participants: the city of Amsterdam, the Van Aerssen van Sommelsdijck family and the Dutch West India Company. All Dutch citizens could trade with Suriname, and planters were consulted in a Council of Police, a feature the text calls unique among the Guyana colonies. The Batavian Republic nationalised the Society in November 1795.

entries_new.name: Danish East India Company
entries_new.mechanism: A royal charter plus a treaty with a local ruler gave a company a fortified trading town.
entries_new.story: The Danish East India Company refers to two Danish-Norwegian chartered companies, the first from 1616 to 1650 and the second from 1670 to 1729. Under a treaty of 19 November 1620 the ruler of Tanjore, Raghunatha Nayak, gave the Danes the town of Tranquebar in India, where they built Dansborg. The first company lost all acquisitions except Tranquebar. Dansborg was ceded to the second company in 1670. The second company was dissolved in 1729 and re-founded in 1730 as the Asiatic Company.

entries_new.name: Danish West India Company
entries_new.mechanism: A royal charter gave a company the right to settle and govern Caribbean islands.
entries_new.story: The Danish West India Company, also called the West India-Guinea Company, was a Dano-Norwegian chartered company formally chartered by King Christian V on 11 March 1671. The Danes settled St Thomas in 1668, bought St John in 1718 and St Croix from the French in 1733. It also traded on the Danish Gold Coast, and an estimated 120,000 enslaved Africans were carried on its ships. The company governed the colonies until 1754, when the Danish government's Chamber of Revenues took control.

entries_new.name: Sierra Leone Company
entries_new.founder: Granville Sharp, Henry Thornton, Thomas Clarkson and others
entries_new.mechanism: An Act of Parliament, not a royal charter, incorporated a company to run a settlement.
entries_new.story: The Sierra Leone Company was the body that founded the second British colony in Africa on 11 March 1792. It was set up under the Sierra Leone Company Act 1791 after attempts to win a royal charter failed. In 1792 John Clarkson led over 1,100 Black settlers from Halifax, Nova Scotia, most of them former slaves of the American colonies freed by the British, to found Freetown. Slave-trade merchants and West India planters petitioned against the bill, which passed Parliament 87 votes to 9.

entries_new.name: Van Diemen's Land Company
entries_new.challenge: Peerapper people, who were killed or removed
entries_new.mechanism: A royal charter and an Act of Parliament gave a company a large land grant to farm.
entries_new.story: The Van Diemen's Land Company is a farming company in Tasmania, founded in 1825 with a royal charter and granted 250,000 acres in the north-west of the island in 1826. By 1828 the grant was increased to 350,000 acres in several large blocks. Its manager Edward Curr is quoted as saying the land could only be held by exterminating or expelling the Peerapper people. The text states that company employees carried out massacres, including at Cape Grim, and that by 1835 the Peerapper were gone from the region. Parts of the land were sold in 2016 and 2021.

entries_new.name: Canada Company
entries_new.mechanism: A royal charter let a company buy and resell the unsettled lands of a colony.
entries_new.story: The Canada Company was a British land company incorporated by royal charter on 19 August 1826. In 1827 it bought the undeveloped clergy and Crown reserves of Upper Canada for 341,000 pounds. Its main project was the Huron Tract, which it surveyed, divided into lots, and advertised to buyers in Europe, laying out Goderich on Lake Huron as the centre. The settlement dispossessed the Mississauga people of their ancestral lands. John Galt, the first superintendent, founded Guelph. The company voted to wind up on 12 August 1953 and was dissolved on 18 December 1953.

entries_new.name: South Australian Company
entries_new.mechanism: A private firm met the land-purchase condition of a colonisation Act, which allowed settlement to start.
entries_new.story: The South Australian Company was formed in London on 9 October 1835 after the 1834 Act created the Province of South Australia. It was a commercial firm unconnected to the government or the Colonisation Commission, led by George Fife Angas, and it bought unsold land to the level the Act required so emigration could start. In 1836 four ships settled Kingscote on Kangaroo Island, and the company then moved to the mainland, providing basic infrastructure and selling or leasing land to immigrants. It was wound up on 17 March 1949.

entries_new.name: Eastern Archipelago Company
entries_new.recognition: British Crown; Sultan of Brunei rights
entries_new.mechanism: Coal rights obtained from a Bornean sultan were turned into a royal charter for land and mining on an island.
entries_new.story: The Eastern Archipelago Company was incorporated by British royal charter in 1847 and was active on the island of Labuan, off the coast of Borneo, until it was dissolved in 1858. Henry Wise, a former East India Company maritime officer, had acquired the coal rights from James Brooke, the White Rajah of Sarawak, who had obtained them from the Sultan of Brunei. The charter let the company buy, hold, settle and sell land on Labuan and nearby, mine coal and trade with the island's inhabitants.

entries_new.name: German New Guinea Company
entries_new.mechanism: An imperial charter delegated rule of a protectorate to a private company.
entries_new.story: The German New Guinea Company was founded in Berlin in 1884 by Adolph von Hansemann and a syndicate of bankers to colonise and exploit north-eastern New Guinea and nearby islands. Chancellor Bismarck ordered a protectorate on 19 August of that year. For the first fifteen years the colony was run under imperial charters by the private company. From 1899 to 1914 the German government administered German New Guinea through a governor. The government's priority was rapid economic development based on a German-controlled plantation economy.

entries_new.name: German East Africa Company
entries_new.founder: Carl Peters, among its principal founders
entries_new.recognition: German Empire; Sultan of Zanzibar lease
entries_new.mechanism: A lease from a sultan plus a German charter gave a company the right to administer a coastal strip.
entries_new.story: The German East Africa Company originated in 1884 as the Society for German Colonisation. In April 1885 it leased the coastal strip opposite Zanzibar from Sultan Khalifa bin Said for 50 years. Its attempt to take over administration provoked a general revolt along the coast of what is now Tanzania. The company held Dar es Salaam and Bagamoyo only with help from the German navy, and in 1889 asked the government to put the rebellion down. In 1891 it sold out to the German government, which then ruled German East Africa directly.

entries_new.name: German West African Company
entries_new.mechanism: A charter gave a company commercial rights in two protectorates without governing powers.
entries_new.story: The German West African Company was a German chartered company founded in 1885 with headquarters in Hamburg. It exploited the two German protectorates of Togo and Cameroon but, unlike its counterpart in German East Africa, did not actually govern them. After years of little profit, the German Empire absorbed the company on 13 November 1903.

entries_new.name: Mozambique Company
entries_new.mechanism: A Portuguese royal charter handed tax collection, labour and land rights over two provinces to a company.
entries_new.story: The Mozambique Company held a 50-year concession over the lands of what are now Manica and Sofala provinces in central Mozambique. It was set up on 11 February 1891 with capital from German, British and South African financiers. It had the exclusive right to collect taxes, could grant sub-concessions, and used forced labour (the chibalo system). Resistance to forced labour led to rebellions against it in 1902 and 1917. Under the Salazar regime, Portugal did not renew the concession, and on 18 July 1942 the territory passed to the colonial administration.

entries_new.name: Niassa Company
entries_new.mechanism: A Portuguese royal charter gave a company rule and taxation of two northern provinces.
entries_new.story: The Niassa Company, also called the Nyassa Chartered Company, held a concession from 1891 to 1929 over the current Cabo Delgado and Niassa provinces of Mozambique, more than 160,000 square kilometres between the Ruvuma and Lúrio rivers. The Portuguese government issued the formal charter in March 1893. Its founder's syndicate failed to raise capital, so French and British investors bought the concession and moved headquarters to London. The company relied on a hut tax, raised from 2 escudos in 1921 to 85 in 1929. The concession ended on 27 October 1929, with the company owing over a million pounds.

entries_new.name: Russian-American Company
entries_new.challenge: Britain and the United States disputed its southern border
entries_new.mechanism: An imperial decree gave one company a monopoly and rule over Russian America.
entries_new.story: The Russian-American Company was a state-sponsored chartered company created by Emperor Paul's decree of 1799 to settle Russian America, trade with Indigenous people and expand colonisation. Its monopoly originally ran south to 55 degrees North, later claimed to 51 degrees North, a border challenged by Britain and the United States and settled in the treaties of 1824 and 1825. Alexander Baranov founded Pavlovskaya and New Archangel (now Sitka). Aleut and Alutiiq men were forcibly conscripted to work for it. Alaska was sold to the United States in 1867.

entries_new.name: Company of Scotland (Darien scheme)
entries_new.founder: William Paterson led the Darien scheme
entries_new.mechanism: An act of the Scottish Parliament gave a company monopoly rights and sovereign powers overseas.
entries_new.story: The Company of Scotland Trading to Africa and the Indies, also called the Scottish Darien Company, was created by an act of the Parliament of Scotland in 1695, with a monopoly of Scottish trade to India, Africa and the Americas, sovereign rights and 21 years of tax exemption. In July 1698 it sent five ships and 1,200 colonists to Darien on the Isthmus of Panama. The settlement was poorly supplied and abandoned; a second expedition was besieged by Spain, and more than a thousand died of hunger and disease. The venture drained an estimated quarter of Scotland's liquid assets and helped lead to the Act of Union 1707.

entries_new.name: Company of One Hundred Associates
entries_new.mechanism: A royal charter gave investors a fur-trade monopoly in return for settling a colony.
entries_new.story: The Company of One Hundred Associates, formally the Company of New France, was chartered in 1627 under Cardinal Richelieu to run the fur trade and to administer and expand French colonies in North America, centred on the Saint Lawrence valley. In return it was to settle French Catholics there. Each of 100 investors put in 3,000 livres. Samuel de Champlain was its commander in New France from 1629 to 1635. War with England and conflict with the Iroquois hurt it. In 1663 Louis XIV dissolved the company and made New France a province.
